claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 can initially exist as a single-phase high-temperature BCC alloy.
Sluggish Al diffusion maintains the high-temperature BCC phase.
Al-related pairwise interactions kinetically suppress the thermodynamic drive toward phase separation.
Extended holding at lower temperatures permits atomic rearrangement and transformation into secondary phases.
Samples should be annealed at 600–800°C for varied hold times and compared with rapidly quenched samples.
The comparison should use an inert atmosphere and specimens with identical starting compositions and microstructures.
Al causes lattice distortions that lower atomic mobility.
Atomic pairwise interactions control nucleation barriers for secondary phases.
At lower temperatures, thermodynamics slightly favor secondary phases such as L12 or sigma structures.
Al has a high diffusion activation energy in this alloy.
The high activation energy for Al diffusion kinetically delays the BCC-to-secondary-phase transformation.
Coupled interactions of Al with Cr, Co, Fe, and Ni may contribute to delayed transformation.
Prolonged annealing at 600–800°C will gradually decompose the BCC phase into secondary phases.
Rapid cooling will preserve the single-phase BCC state.
As-cast or rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 has a uniform BCC structure.
The proposed mechanism applies below the original BCC stability threshold where diffusion is moderately activated.
Extremely high temperatures or nonthermal mechanical interventions may override the proposed kinetic limitation.
The activation energies, interaction energies, and relative thermodynamic and kinetic contributions have not been quantitatively determined.
XRD, TEM, and atom-probe tomography can be used to measure secondary-phase formation and elemental redistribution.
Failure to observe a statistically significant emergence of secondary phases after extended annealing would falsify the proposed kinetic-suppression mechanism.
